answers.answer: A compass keeps a fixed opening (the radius) while its tip stays at the center, so every point it draws is the same distance from the center.
solution: Put the tip of the compass at the center M.
Set the opening equal to the radius, for example MA.
Turn the pencil around; the opening does not change.
So all points drawn are at the same distance from M, which makes a circle.

answers.answer: The axis of a segment is the straight line perpendicular to it at its midpoint.
solution: Find the midpoint F of the segment.
Draw the line L perpendicular to the segment through F.
This line L is the axis of the segment, where L ∩ AB = {F}.

answers.answer: Yes
solution: The center of the circle is on the axis of the chord AB.
This is true for any chord of the circle.
So the center lies on the axis of any chord in it.

answers.answer: A circle is identified by giving its center and its radius length.
solution: Know the center of the circle.
Know the radius length.
Place the compass tip at the center, open it to the radius, and draw the circle.

answers.answer: An infinite number of points; an infinite number of circles
solution: The plane has an infinite number of points.
Each chosen point can be a center M, and the circle with radius MA passes through A.
So an infinite number of circles pass through A.

answers.answer: On a congruent circle whose center is point A
solution: Equal radii means each center is the same distance from A.
So the centers lie on a circle with center A and the same radius.
This circle is congruent to those circles.

answers.answer: An infinite number of circles
solution: Choose a point M at distance 2 cm from A.
Put the compass tip at M with opening 2 cm and draw the circle; it passes through A.
Any point on the circle with center A and radius 2 cm can be the center M.
Keep the arcs.
The centers are on a congruent circle with center A, so there are an infinite number of circles.

answers.answer: The line L has an infinite number of points; an infinite number of circles pass through A and B
solution: L is the axis of AB and has an infinite number of points.
Each point E on L is a center of a circle passing through A and B.
So an infinite number of circles pass through A and B.

answers.answer: 1/2 AB
solution: The smallest circle through A and B has AB as its diameter.
So its radius equals half the length of AB.

answers.answer: No
solution: Two circles cannot intersect in more than two points.

answers.answer: No, M cannot be identified: no such point M exists, because A, B and C are collinear and no circle passes through them.
solution: If L1 ∩ L2 = φ, then L1 is parallel to L2.
This happens when A, B and C are collinear.
The center M must be on both L1 and L2, but they never meet.
So there is no point M, and no circle can pass through A, B and C.

answers.answer: Triangle ABC is acute-angled, and the center of the circle is inside the triangle.
solution: Draw AB = 4 cm.
With the compass tip at A and opening 6 cm draw an arc; with the tip at B and opening 5 cm draw another arc. Their intersection is C.
Join AC and BC.
Draw L1, the axis of AB, and L2, the axis of BC.
Mark M where L1 ∩ L2 = {M}.
With the tip at M and opening MA, draw the circle through A, B and C.
The longest side is 6 cm and 6² = 36 is less than 4² + 5² = 41, so all angles are acute.
The triangle is acute-angled and the center M is inside the triangle.

The axis of a segment is the straight line perpendicular to it at its midpoint (its perpendicular bisector). Every point on it is equidistant from the segment's endpoints.
Yes. The center is equidistant from the endpoints of any chord, so it lies on the axis (perpendicular bisector) of that chord.

The plane has infinitely many points. Infinitely many circles can be drawn through A, one for each chosen center.
Their centers lie on a circle whose center is A and whose radius equals that common radius (a circle congruent to them).
Infinitely many circles (each center is a point on the circle of radius 2 cm centered at A).

Drawing: triangle ABC with AB = 4 cm, BC = 5 cm, CA = 6 cm, plus its circumcircle. The center is where the perpendicular bisectors of two sides meet. Since $6^2 = 36 < 4^2 + 5^2 = 41$, the triangle is acute-angled. The center of the circle is inside the triangle.
2 circles
solution: Draw AB = 4 cm. Diameter 5 cm, so radius = 5 ÷ 2 = 2.5 cm.
Draw L, the axis of AB. The center of any circle through A and B lies on L.
Set the compass opening to 2.5 cm, put the tip at A and draw an arc that cuts L. It cuts L at two points, one on each side of AB. Call them M and M₁.
The compass opening 2.5 cm is more than half of AB (2 cm), so the arc does cut L.
Put the tip at M and draw the circle of radius 2.5 cm. It passes through A and B. Do the same at M₁.
There are 2 possible circles, with centers M and M₁ on the axis of AB on opposite sides of AB.

answers.answer: 1 circle (its center is the midpoint of AB and AB is its diameter)
solution: Draw AB = 4 cm. Half of AB = 2 cm.
The smallest circle through A and B has radius ½AB = 2 cm.
The given radius 2 cm equals this smallest radius, so only that smallest circle works.
Its center is F, the midpoint of AB, where the axis L meets AB.
Put the tip at F, open the compass to 2 cm and draw the circle. It passes through A and B.
There is only 1 possible circle.

answers.answer: No circle is possible
solution: Draw AB = 4 cm. Diameter 3 cm, so radius = 3 ÷ 2 = 1.5 cm.
The smallest circle through A and B has radius ½AB = 2 cm.
1.5 cm is less than 2 cm, so the radius is too small.
A compass opening of 1.5 cm from A does not reach the axis of AB, so no center can be found.
No circle with diameter 3 cm passes through A and B, so there is no solution.

answers.answer: Two solutions: the radius is 2.5 cm, so the center lies on the axis of AB at distance 1.5 cm from the midpoint F of AB, on either side of AB. That gives two circles.
One solution: the radius 2 cm is half of AB, so the center is the midpoint F of AB and AB is a diameter. That gives exactly one circle.
No solution: the diameter 3 cm is less than AB = 4 cm. The smallest circle through A and B has diameter 4 cm, so no such circle exists.
